analysis.one_liner: Blocks the Treasury from writing rules that close a corporate tax loophole involving foreign "hybrid" entities.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred the Treasury from cracking down on tax-avoidance structures used by multinational corporations, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Treasury Department from issuing regulations, announced in IRS Notice 98-35, designed to stop multinational corporations from using "hybrid" foreign-entity structures to avoid U.S. tax on foreign income. Instead of letting the tax agency act, it would require a study, a public hearing, and a report to Congress first. The bill never got past the Senate Finance Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational corporations that structure overseas operations through hybrid foreign entities would benefit, because the IRS rules they would dodge were aimed at preventing these structures from escaping subpart F taxation of foreign income. Ordinary taxpayers who do not use such structures would bear a slightly larger share of the tax burden to make up for revenue the loophole shelters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Multinationals using hybrid foreign tax structures

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbade the Treasury Secretary from issuing the temporary or final regulations contemplated by IRS Notice 98-35, which targeted 'hybrid' arrangements — foreign-entity structures corporations use to escape subpart F rules that tax certain foreign income of controlled foreign corporations.

It also ordered the Treasury to withdraw retroactively any such regulations issued in the meantime, and barred changes to the entity-classification rules that would alter the treatment of hybrid transactions.
In place of regulation, it required a Treasury study, at least one public hearing, and a report to the congressional tax committees.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers generally, who would shoulder more of the tax burden if corporate foreign income continues to escape U.S. taxation through hybrid structures.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override Treasury and IRS Notice 98-35, blocking the government from reining in 'hybrid' structures that multinational corporations use to avoid U.S. tax on foreign income — a direct cost to the federal tax base that ordinary taxpayers ultimately support.

Supporters would argue the bill preserved due process: it required Treasury to study the issue, hold a public hearing, and report to Congress before any rules, on the theory that taxpayers should not face retroactive or unexplained regulatory change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated rationale was procedural — giving the public notice and a hearing before the tax rules on international transactions were rewritten — which is a fair-sounding concern. But its actual effect would have been to block the IRS from closing a loophole that multinational corporations use to shift income offshore, at the expense of the tax base ordinary taxpayers fund. The one-month study-and-hearing requirement does not offset a prohibition on the rules themselves. The Congress ending without a vote spared the Treasury's anti-abuse effort from this restriction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never taken up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 1, 1998 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No further action followed: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no action in the House before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The IRS and Treasury kept authority under Notice 98-35 to pursue corporate tax avoidance through hybrid foreign-entity structures, since the bill blocking them died in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and tax enforcement; not the bill's backers

for.name: Sen. John Breaux
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar Treasury from issuing the hybrid-transaction regulations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and never advanced far enough for a party split to show; it died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked the IRS from using 'hybrid' entity rules to tax foreign income that companies structure through foreign affiliates, keeping a tax-avoidance channel open. That cost is ultimately borne by other taxpayers.

The bill would strip the Treasury of authority to write rules addressing hybrid transactions and force it to withdraw any such rules retroactively, deferring the policy question to a study and report.
